payload.throughline: Track charge at each electrode, decide whether the cell supplies or consumes electrical work, and connect that bookkeeping to voltage, electrolysis, concentration, and rechargeable batteries.

learner_content_blocks: Starting check: use the supplied half-reactions to locate electron production and electron consumption. If half-reaction balancing or mole ratios are not secure, use the prerequisite handoff before continuing.
Goal: identify the anode, cathode, oxidation, reduction, electrolyte role, and electron-flow direction without relying on electrode sign alone.
Bridge: the prerequisite lesson supplies balanced redox half-reactions and stoichiometric coefficients. This lesson uses those records to organize a complete cell.
Oxidation always occurs at the anode and produces electrons. Reduction always occurs at the cathode and consumes electrons. External-circuit electrons therefore travel from anode to cathode.

A galvanic cell drives a spontaneous redox reaction: its anode is negative and cathode positive. An electrolytic cell is driven by a power source: its anode is positive and cathode negative. The chemistry labels do not reverse when the signs do.
The electrolyte carries ions inside the cell to limit charge buildup; electrons travel through the external conductor, not through the electrolyte.

Use a four-line ledger: write oxidation and released electrons at the anode; write reduction and accepted electrons at the cathode; draw external electrons anode → cathode; only then assign signs from the stated cell type.

For Zn(s) → Zn2+ + 2 e− and Cu2+ + 2 e− → Cu(s), I choose the zinc electrode as the anode because its half-reaction releases electrons. I choose copper as the cathode because its half-reaction consumes them. Since the cell is galvanic, zinc is negative, copper is positive, and electrons move through the wire from zinc to copper. I did not start from memorized signs because that would fail in an electrolytic cell.

Worked example: an external source drives molten MgCl2. At the cathode, Mg2+ + 2 e− → Mg; at the anode, 2 Cl− → Cl2 + 2 e−. The source pushes electrons toward the cathode and removes them from the anode. Reduction is still cathodic and oxidation still anodic even though the electrolytic cathode is negative and anode positive.
Guided practice: first mark which supplied half-reaction releases electrons, then label that electrode before considering polarity.
Less help: classify both electrodes and trace the external electron path from two new half-reactions.
On your own: use reaction direction and stated cell type to assign electrode identity and sign.
Boundary: anode does not mean negative. It means oxidation. Negative anode applies to a galvanic cell; a driven electrolytic cell has a positive anode.
Non-example: saying electrons cross the salt bridge confuses ionic charge balance with the external electronic current.
Near exit: solve a fresh galvanic-cell bookkeeping problem with no answer-bearing support.
Changed exit: switch to an externally driven cell and preserve the oxidation/anode and reduction/cathode relationships while electrode signs change.

Repair the near-use function: ignore the electrode names first. Circle the half-reaction that writes electrons as products; that location is the anode and the starting point of external electron flow.
Fresh re-entry: apply the same half-reaction-to-electrode function to a new metal pair and untouched option family.

Repair the changed-task function: keep the chemical labels fixed, then add the cell-type sign convention. In an electrolytic cell, the power source pulls electrons from the positive anode and supplies the negative cathode.
Fresh re-entry: classify a different driven reaction without reusing the exposed substances, values, or answer pattern.
Recap: chemistry names come from electron bookkeeping; signs come from cell type. Anode = oxidation = electron source, cathode = reduction = electron sink.
Starting check: compare two tabulated reduction potentials and identify which reduction is more favorable under the stated standard conditions.
Goal: construct a galvanic-cell potential from a reduction-potential table and use its sign to check the chosen reaction direction.
Bridge: the preceding microcycle established anode, cathode, and electron flow. Here, numerical reduction potentials choose which listed half-reaction runs as reduction.
Tables list reduction potentials. For the chosen cell direction, E°cell = E°reduction at the cathode − E°reduction listed for the anode.

Do not multiply a reduction potential when multiplying a half-reaction to balance electrons. Potential is energy per unit charge, so stoichiometric scaling changes electron count but not the tabulated voltage.
A positive E°cell supports a spontaneous galvanic direction under the stated standard conditions; a negative result means the written direction is nonspontaneous under those conditions.

Use choose–subtract–check: choose the higher listed reduction potential as the galvanic cathode, subtract the other listed reduction potential, then check that the result is positive and electron flow runs from the lower-potential oxidation side to the higher-potential reduction side.

Given Ag+ + e− → Ag at +0.80 V and Zn2+ + 2 e− → Zn at −0.76 V, I choose silver reduction at the cathode. I calculate 0.80 − (−0.76) = +1.56 V. I balance electrons in the equations but do not double +0.80 V.

Worked example: Cu2+/Cu is +0.34 V and Fe2+/Fe is −0.44 V. Copper is reduced, iron is oxidized, and E°cell = 0.34 − (−0.44) = +0.78 V. Electrons therefore leave iron and reach copper through the wire.
Guided practice: mark the higher reduction potential, label it cathode, and substitute both listed values into cathode minus anode.
Less help: select the galvanic direction and calculate the potential from a fresh two-row table.
On your own: reject a reaction direction whose calculated standard potential is negative.
Boundary: multiplying a half-reaction coefficient does not multiply its reduction potential.
Non-example: adding two listed reduction potentials without reversing the sign logic can produce a number that is not the potential of the chosen cell reaction.
Near exit: calculate a fresh standard galvanic potential and electron direction from two listed reductions.
Changed exit: evaluate the reverse written reaction and decide whether external electrical input is required under the same stated conditions.
Repair the near-use function: label cathode and anode on the table before touching signs; then use listed cathode reduction minus listed anode reduction.
Fresh re-entry: compute a new galvanic pair with different potentials and a different keyed position.
Repair the changed-task function: reversing the overall reaction reverses the sign of E°cell. A negative value for the written direction signals that it must be driven under the stated conditions.
Fresh re-entry: test a new reversed direction without reusing the exposed potential pair.
Recap: tables stay in reduction form; choose the cathode, subtract the anode's listed reduction potential, never scale voltage by coefficients, and check reaction direction with the sign.
Starting check: connect current and time to charge before attempting deposition stoichiometry.
Goal: predict an electrolytic product from the supplied half-reaction and calculate its amount from current and time.
Bridge: prior stoichiometry supplies mole ratios; the preceding cell bookkeeping identifies which half-reaction occurs at each driven electrode.
Electrical charge is Q = It, with amperes equal to coulombs per second. Electron amount is n(e−) = Q/F, using F = 9.65 × 10^4 C per mole of electrons when supplied.
The half-reaction coefficient converts moles of electrons to moles of deposited metal or liberated gas. Multiply by molar mass only after finding product moles.
Product identity comes from the stated electrolysis conditions and supplied half-reactions; charge determines amount, not which competing reaction is selected.
Follow a unit ladder: amperes × seconds → coulombs → moles e− → moles product → grams or gas amount. Write the electron-to-product ratio beside the half-reaction before calculating.
For Ag+ + e− → Ag, 9.65 × 10^3 C is 0.100 mol e− and therefore 0.100 mol Ag. For Cu2+ + 2 e− → Cu, that same charge gives only 0.0500 mol Cu. The electron coefficient is the decision point.

Worked example: a 5.00 A current runs for 1930 s through a cell where Ni2+ + 2 e− → Ni is the cathode reaction. Q = 9650 C = 0.100 mol e−, so 0.0500 mol Ni forms. With 58.7 g/mol supplied, the mass is 2.94 g.
Guided practice: calculate charge first, then annotate the electron coefficient in the supplied deposition half-reaction.
Less help: move from charge to moles of a divalent metal deposit.
On your own: distinguish electron moles from product moles in a gas-liberation reaction.
Boundary: equal charge transfers equal moles of electrons, not equal moles or masses of every product.
Non-example: using current without time leaves coulombs undetermined and cannot support a product amount.
Near exit: calculate a fresh metal deposit from current, time, Faraday's constant, and a supplied half-reaction.
Changed exit: solve backward for electrolysis time when a target gas amount and current are specified.
Repair the near-use function: write Q = It with seconds, divide by F once, then apply the electron coefficient before molar mass.
Fresh re-entry: calculate deposition for a different ion charge and untouched numerical values.
Repair the changed-task function: begin from desired product moles, convert backward to electron moles and charge, then divide by current to obtain time.
Fresh re-entry: determine time for a different gas half-reaction and current.
Recap: electrolysis amount is a charge ledger: It, then Q/F, then the half-reaction ratio, then any requested mass or time conversion.
Starting check: distinguish a concentration difference from a difference in electrode identity.
Goal: predict the direction that reduces a metal-ion concentration difference in a same-metal concentration cell.
Bridge: electrode redox bookkeeping still controls electron flow. The new feature is that identical half-cells differ in concentration rather than substance.
For a metal/metal-ion concentration cell with identical electrodes, the concentration difference creates the potential. The spontaneous direction tends to reduce that difference.

At the dilute side, metal oxidation M(s) → M^n+ + n e− adds ions. At the concentrated side, M^n+ + n e− → M(s) consumes ions. Electrons therefore move from the dilute-side anode to the concentrated-side cathode under the stated model.
This lesson uses qualitative direction only; it does not import the Nernst equation as a required core calculation.
Imagine a concentration seesaw: oxidation raises the dilute ion side; reduction lowers the concentrated ion side. The electron arrow connects those two balancing actions.

With Cu/Cu2+ on both sides, 0.010 M and 1.0 M, I ask which changes narrow the gap. Oxidation on the 0.010 M side creates Cu2+, while reduction on the 1.0 M side removes Cu2+. So the dilute side is anode and electrons travel dilute → concentrated.

Worked example: two Ag/Ag+ half-cells contain 0.020 M and 0.50 M Ag+. Silver metal dissolves at the 0.020 M side, depositing electrons into the wire; Ag+ plates at the 0.50 M side. As the cell operates, the concentrations move toward one another.
Guided practice: mark which half-cell must create ions and which must consume them to narrow the supplied concentration gap.
Less help: assign dilute-side and concentrated-side electrode roles.
On your own: predict how both concentrations change while the cell discharges.
Boundary: this qualitative rule is for the stated same-metal metal/metal-ion concentration cell. It is not a universal rule for every possible concentration-driven electrochemical system.
Non-example: selecting a direction by comparing electrode materials fails because the two electrodes are chemically identical.
Near exit: assign anode, cathode, electron direction, and concentration changes in a fresh same-metal cell.
Changed exit: infer how reversing the initial concentration labels reverses the electrode roles without changing the metal identity.
Repair the near-use function: write oxidation as ion creation and reduction as ion consumption, then place each where it narrows the gap.
Fresh re-entry: apply the same narrowing function to a different metal and concentration pair.
Repair the changed-task function: electrode identity does not fix the role; the currently dilute side oxidizes and the currently concentrated side reduces.
Fresh re-entry: reassign roles after a new concentration reversal using untouched values.
Recap: identical electrodes can still make a cell. Oxidation raises the dilute ion side, reduction lowers the concentrated ion side, and electrons flow dilute → concentrated.
Starting check: distinguish a single electrochemical cell from a battery assembled from multiple cells.
Goal: connect named rechargeable-battery chemistry to discharge direction, cell voltage, series voltage, and externally driven recharge.
Bridge: galvanic bookkeeping describes discharge; electrolytic bookkeeping describes the externally driven reverse direction during recharge.
A battery combines one or more electrochemical cells. Cells connected in series add their voltages; capacity and delivered current depend on additional design facts not inferred from voltage alone.

During lead-acid discharge, Pb is oxidized and PbO2 is reduced; both electrodes form PbSO4, and sulfuric acid is consumed as water forms. A typical lead-acid cell is about 2 V, so six series cells provide about 12 V.

During nickel-cadmium discharge, Cd is oxidized and nickel oxyhydroxide is reduced toward nickel hydroxide in alkaline electrolyte. Recharge applies external electrical work to drive the net discharge reactions in reverse.

Use two layers: inside each cell, track the discharge redox pair; across the battery, add series cell voltages. For recharge, reverse the net chemical direction only because an external source supplies energy.

For a six-cell lead-acid battery, I use about 2 V per cell to predict about 12 V. If discharge data show sulfuric acid concentration falling, that matches acid consumption as both electrodes move toward PbSO4. I do not infer remaining capacity from voltage alone.

Worked example: three 1.2 V nickel-cadmium cells in series provide about 3.6 V. During discharge, cadmium is the oxidation site and the nickel oxyhydroxide electrode is reduced. A charger supplies electrical work to reverse the net reaction; simply reconnecting identical terminals does not create recharge.
Guided practice: separate the per-cell chemistry question from the series-voltage calculation.
Less help: identify the lead-acid discharge product shared by both electrodes.
On your own: classify discharge as galvanic and recharge as externally driven reverse chemistry.
Boundary: voltage is not capacity. Adding series cells raises total voltage, but the prompt must supply other information before inferring run time or stored charge.
Non-example: assuming recharge is spontaneous ignores the external work needed to reverse the discharge reaction.
Near exit: combine named lead-acid discharge chemistry with a fresh series-voltage calculation.
Changed exit: diagnose a nickel-cadmium recharge scenario by tracking which discharge half-reaction must be driven in reverse.
Repair the near-use function: make one row for cell chemistry and a separate row for number of series cells × voltage per cell.
Fresh re-entry: apply the same two-layer reasoning to a different lead-acid series configuration.
Repair the changed-task function: write the discharge oxidation and reduction first, then reverse the net directions only when an external charger is present.
Fresh re-entry: analyze a new nickel-cadmium charging fault without reusing the exposed reaction cue.
Recap: named chemistry determines discharge products and electrode roles; series connection adds voltage; recharge is an externally driven reversal, and voltage alone does not establish capacity.
